Carlos — thanks for the sample, very helpful. High level up front: Redwood bills per-token, but the runtime will not double-bill repeated KV-prefix tokens when KV reuse is possible. That said, the billing rules depend on deployment and package: hosted customers get automatic prefix/KV reuse across requests in the same session window; Dedicated/Private customers can pin cache affinity for even stronger reuse.

Quick answers:
- Prefix reuse: in your sample, repeated template headers (the 40–80 token prefixes) will be deduplicated at the runtime level where the KV cache is warm. Billing-wise we charge for the initial warm-up tokens and then for the incremental tokens per request; we do not retroactively credit earlier calls. Example: if the first call consumes 80 prefix + 60 body = 140 tokens, and subsequent call with same prefix uses 60 tokens only, you'll be billed 140 + 60.
- Rounding/minimums: hosted API uses a per-call floor of 32 token-units (for microcalls) but aggregates for 6-minute session windows to give you effective smoothing. Dedicated contracts commonly negotiate a per-request floor waiver in exchange for commit bands.

I'll map a few rows from your CSV below to make this concrete; see attached example calculations. If BlueJar prefers predictability, we can propose a hybrid: committed token band + a discounted per-call microfloor waiver for the first 18 months.

Next steps: tessa, can you draft two packaging options (committed band + microfloor waiver vs. session-commit model) and attach estimated TCO for the sample? Aditya — quick check on the KV credit behavior for Dedicated customers (we want to ensure the wording matches the runtime guarantee).

— Kimberly Park

Carlos/Kimberly — attaching two packaging sketches inline. I kept the math conservative.

Option A: Committed token band + microfloor waiver
- Commit: 15M tokens / month at 12% discount off list
- Microfloor: waive 32-token per-call floor for up to 1M calls/month (ensure microcalls priced at true per-token rate)
- KV warm-up credit: 5% credit applied to the first 1M tokens of KV-warm workload per month (to offset initial prefix cost)

Option B: Session-commit model (good if >60% of calls are repeated prefixes)
- Commit: 10M tokens / month + 2K reserved concurrent sessions
- Effective per-token discount: 18% off list due to commit + cache affinity
- Rounding: We aggregate per-session over a 10-minute window and bill on total tokens (so microcalls absorb into the session bucket)

Estimated impact on your sample: Option A reduces month 1 spend by ~9% (warm-up still visible). Option B reduces month 1 spend by ~15% but requires minimal engineering for session affinity.

Contracts note: Option B needs explicit cache-affinity SLA to be in the SOW. If you want, I can prototype a short MAP (mutual action plan) showing the engineering changes and expected delta.

Quick engineering clarifications from runtime/serve team:
- KV cache semantics: cache keys are per-model + per-prefix-hash when affinity is enabled. For Hosted customers we maintain an LRU global cache; for Dedicated we pin hot prefixes to the pod group which yields much higher reuse.
- Billing crediting: we do not retroactively credit previously billed warm-up tokens; instead we issue a KV-warmup rebate (percent of billed tokens) during the first billing cycle of a negotiated commit. The rebate appears as a line item on the invoice.
- Aggregation windows: Hosted = 6-minute window for session aggregation; Dedicated = negotiable, default 10 minutes if session affinity is requested. Aggregation means we sum tokens across the window then apply rounding/minimums once to the aggregated total.
- Edge case: interleaved templates per user (user rotates templates within the same session) reduce reuse; we can estimate an effective reuse factor from your CSV if you want.

For BlueJar: if you plan to shard templates by user (one template per flow) and keep sessions alive, your effective billed tokens should drop ~25–40% vs naive per-call billing. I'll run the sample through the reuse estimator if you confirm you'd like that.

— Aditya Rao
